question:
Patient note:
A 53-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus, well-controlled hypertension, and class II obesity was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after awakening at home with excruciating pain, swelling, and erythema of the medial left thigh that had progressed over the preceding twelve hours to dusky discoloration with rapidly advancing borders and serosanguinous bullae; his spouse reported that he had gone to bed the prior evening complaining of a “pulled muscle” after landscaping work but awoke drenched in sweat, febrile, and confused about the date. On arrival—before receiving antibiotics, fluids, or analgesia—he appeared toxic and diaphoretic, sat upright on the stretcher, and was breathing through a tight-fitting Venturi mask set to deliver 50 % inspired oxygen because pulse oximetry on room air had fallen to 78 % during transport. Initial noninvasive blood pressure measured 112/65 mm Hg, radial pulse was bounding at 122 beats per minute in regular rhythm, and respiratory rate was 31 breaths per minute with shallow tidal volumes and visible intercostal retractions. Core temperature obtained via Foley catheter read 39.6 °C. Neurologically he opened eyes spontaneously, followed commands, but was disoriented to month, generating a Glasgow Coma Score of 14. Extremities were warm yet mottled distally, capillary refill was four seconds, and the left thigh lesion extended from the groin crease to mid-femur with crepitus and exquisite tenderness; no peripheral edema, jugular venous distention, or organomegaly was present. Cardiopulmonary examination revealed tachycardia without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; bilateral breath sounds were coarse with faint crackles at the bases, consistent with evolving inflammatory lung involvement rather than cardiogenic edema, and no wheezes or rhonchi were auscultated. An arterial blood gas drawn fifteen minutes after arrival on the cited oxygen concentration demonstrated pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 29 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 70 mm Hg; the calculated alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient was markedly widened at 498 mm Hg, suggesting severe ventilation-perfusion mismatch in the setting of systemic infection. Concurrent basic metabolic panel revealed serum sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, chloride 97 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 20 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, a value consistent with his outpatient baseline documented two months earlier, indicating no superimposed kidney injury. Point-of-care lactate was 4.1 mmol/L. Complete blood count showed white blood cell count 19 000 / mm³ with 88 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 33 %, platelet count 210 000 / µL, and no schistocytes on peripheral smear. Coagulation studies demonstrated an international normalized ratio of 1.2 and fibrinogen 540 mg/dL, while serum glucose was 268 mg/dL without ketones. Chest radiograph obtained before any fluid resuscitation depicted bilateral patchy opacities more prominent in the dependent regions, and soft-tissue plain film of the thigh illustrated subcutaneous gas tracking along fascial planes. Bedside ultrasound of the inferior vena cava showed good collapsibility, arguing against volume overload, and focused transthoracic echocardiogram revealed normal left ventricular systolic function with no valvular abnormalities. Past history was notable only for the conditions above; he has never undergone organ transplantation, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or chronic corticosteroid therapy, and there is no record of advanced liver, lung, or renal disease. He works as a warehouse supervisor, smokes half a pack per day for thirty years, drinks beer on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. Medications at home include metformin, lisinopril, and low-dose aspirin, with no known drug allergies. He had not taken any nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or antibiotics in the days preceding presentation. Family history is remarkable for coronary artery disease in both parents but negative for clotting disorders or connective-tissue disease. Prior to transfer to the intensive care unit, no intravenous fluids, vasopressors, or insulin had yet been started, blood cultures and tissue cultures were still pending, and surgical consultation for emergent debridement had been paged; the physiologic measurements and laboratory values above therefore capture his status at the moment of ICU admission decision.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II sums 12 acute physiology components, age points, and chronic health points. Using the available admission measurements:
• Core temperature 39.6°C (39–40.9): 3.
• Mean arterial pressure ≈ (112 + 2 × 65)/3 = 81 mmHg (70–109): 0.
• Heart rate 122/min (110–139): 2.
• Respiratory rate 31/min (25–34): 1.
• Oxygenation: FiO₂ is 0.50, so use the reported A–a gradient rather than PaO₂. Gradient 498 mmHg (350–499): 3.
• Arterial pH 7.25 (7.25–7.32): 2. Bicarbonate is not scored separately when pH is available.
• Sodium 128 mmol/L (120–129): 2.
• Potassium 4.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.4): 0.
• Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (0.6–1.4), without acute renal failure: 0.
• Hematocrit 33% (30–45.9): 0.
• WBC 19,000/mm³ (15,000–39,999): 1.
• Neurologic points = 15 − GCS = 15 − 14 = 1.
Acute physiology subtotal = 3 + 0 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 15. Age 53 (45–54) adds 2. No qualifying chronic organ insufficiency or immunocompromise is documented: 0.
Total = 15 + 2 + 0 = 17.
Final answer: 17
